summary: Discusses use cases and deployment scenarios for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES), which are services applied to requests or responses at intermediaries. It examines the kinds of things such services could do. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Imagine a helper standing on the road between you and a website who can fix or translate things going by. This lists situations where that is useful.

questions: open pluggable edge services use cases
subtitle: Examples of what OPES services could do to requests and responses, and how they could be deployed.

tldr.problem: The OPES architecture allows services at intermediaries to analyze and transform application-level messages, but it needs concrete examples of what such services are and where they run.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sorts OPES services into those acting on requests, on responses, and those creating responses, then describes surrogate, delegate, enterprise, callout server and chaining deployments.
tldr.outcome: It also gives illustrative failure cases showing how tracing information can tell users and providers where a modification happened. It defines no protocol.

today: RFC 3752 is an Informational document from April 2004 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes use cases and deployment scenarios rather than a protocol.

sections.title: What OPES Is For
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) architecture enables cooperative application services between a data provider, a data consumer, and zero or more OPES processors. These services analyze and possibly transform application-level messages. Filtering rules installed on the processor decide when a service runs, and the service may run locally or on remote callout servers.

This memo collects examples of useful services and of deployment scenarios. The two main scenarios from the OPES architecture are surrogate overlays, which act for data providers, and delegate overlays, which act for data consumers. The authors note that the IAB has expressed architectural and policy concerns in RFC 3238.
sections.eli5: An OPES helper sits between a website and a visitor and can change or check the messages. Rules tell it when to do its job, and it can ask other helpers for hard jobs.

sections.title: Types of OPES Services
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC shows four service activation points in an OPES processor handling HTTP: a request arriving (1), a request leaving (2), a response arriving (3) and a response leaving (4). A data dispatcher examines the rules, enforces policy and invokes service applications at each point.

Services on requests that modify them include parental control, restricting or redirecting access by time of day or employee privileges, hiding the consumer's identity, user agent or referrer, adding user preferences or a device profile, and redirecting requests to reduce server load. Services that do not modify requests include service monitoring, usage tracking for billing, and user profiling with the user's consent.

Services on responses include content adaptation for mobile devices with limited screens and language translation. Logging, monitoring and accounting are examples that leave responses alone. In a caching proxy, an encoding step may happen before storing content and a decoding step before returning it.

Some services create responses, such as assembling a web page with a local weather forecast based on the requestor's preferences, from cached weather data or by embedding a URL that points to another server.
sections.eli5: The helper can look at a question on its way in, or at an answer on its way back, and it can change what it sees or just take notes. Sometimes it even builds the answer itself.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
OPES entities can be deployed on an overlay network, a virtual network layered over an existing IP network to perform application-level services. At the application level this is called an OPES Services Network. Two kinds of parties want these services: delegates, authorized agents acting for data consumers, and surrogates, authorized agents acting for data providers. Parties enforcing policies must communicate them, and are trusted to follow them.

A surrogate overlay has authority to provide services for one or more origin servers (for example dynamic page assembly, watermarking and content adaptation) and sits in the origin server's authoritative domain. A delegate overlay acts for data consumer applications (for example virus scanning and content filtering) and belongs to the consumer's authoritative domain.

In an enterprise, providers and consumers share one administrative and trust domain, so the OPES administrator can enforce corporate policy on all of them. If a callout server outside the corporate firewall is used, for example for translation, the channel must be secure and the server must follow corporate security policies.

Callout servers can share workload or supply specialized services; operations on large objects such as virus scanning are better handled on a dedicated server. Processors can also be chained along the content path, where content passes through several processors in series, or along the callout path, where one processor acts as a content-level switch. Chaining of callout servers is deferred from version 1 of the protocol.
sections.eli5: Some helpers work for the website and some work for the visitor. Inside a company one boss runs everything. A helper can pass heavy jobs to a bigger helper, and helpers can be lined up like an assembly line.

sections.title: Failures and Service Notification
sections.content:
The RFC gives illustrative cases where information about OPES processing helps endpoints learn where and why content was changed. A content provider can probe by requesting its own content and examining trace headers, which may reveal wrong parameters or an unexpected OPES processor in the path.

A requestor who gets a different response than another may report trace text such as "OPES service access control, action: blocked" to the administrator. A user who chose "translate English to Spanish" might see "destination language not supported, no action". A provider unhappy with a translation service might signal "No OPES service #8D3298EB" or "No OPES class language translation" in content headers.

Where an ISP or enterprise applies OPES, the end user can see it but cannot control it. For a content distribution network, a provider's log request is outside the OPES architecture and has its own security implications.
sections.eli5: If a helper changes something, it should leave a note saying so. Then people can tell who did it and ask them to fix it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document presents usage scenarios and deployment cases only. For the overall security of OPES entities it points to the OPES architecture document, which at the time was a work in progress. Trust and policy communication are touched on in the deployment discussion above, but the memo adds no security requirements of its own.
sections.eli5: This note only lists examples. The safety rules for helpers are written in a different document.
